title: Mohammad Sayeef Alam
text:
Professional Experience
Research Assistant in HTA,March 2026 – Present  PenTAG, University of Exeter Exeter, United Kingdom

Appraise industry-submitted Single Technology Appraisal (STA) decision models to inform NICE reimbursement decisions, evaluating the full continuum from economic literature reviews and evidence synthesis to structural modeling, scenario testing, and sensitivity analyses.
Develop de novo HTA decision models and adapt existing NICE models using R and Excel VBA to support Multiple Technology Appraisal (MTA) projects.
Collaborate within multidisciplinary teams including clinicians, epidemiologists, and statisticians to co-author comprehensive evidence assessment reports that directly advise NICE recommendation committees.
Support appraising and conducting Indirect Treatment Comparisons (ITC), conducting ad-hoc analyses, writing manuscripts, and drafting reports used in policy decision-making.
Execute advanced statistical analyses spanning survival analysis, evidence generation, uncertainty quantification, and Delphi studies to deliver tailored solutions for external consultancy clients.

Associate (Advanced Analytics),July 2021 – February 2022  Parexel Remote, India

Developed dynamic R Shiny applications and interactive dashboards for economic evaluations to support HTA submissions and strategic payer decision-making.
Conducted feasibility assessments, indirect treatment comparisons (ITCs), and complete economic analyses for direct integration into HTA dossiers and regulatory/payer submissions.
Designed dashboards to visualize key clinical endpoints, including survival outcomes, treatment sequences, and demographic summaries tailored for regional stakeholder reporting.
Delivered actionable insights to internal and external stakeholders, iteratively incorporating cross-functional feedback to refine deliverables.




Research Experience
PhD Researcher, April 2022 – March 2026  Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU) Trondheim, Norway

Identified 11 celiac disease risk loci by running SAIGE mixed-model GWAS on 17 million variants in ~55,000 participants (~1,100 cases) from the HUNT biobank, correcting for case-control imbalance and relatedness.
Strengthened data quality by applying sample and variant QC to 25 million imputed variants (22 million retained), using KING relatedness estimates and principal components to control population stratification.
Prioritised candidate causal signals by fine-mapping and colocalising the 11 loci, highlighting a non-coding RNA locus near IRX1 suggesting shared immune-mediated genetics with rheumatoid arthritis.
Stratified celiac disease risk by building a Bayesian PRS-CS polygenic risk score (benchmarked against PRSice and LDpred), achieving an AUC of 0.83 in a held-out test set.
Characterised genetic heterogeneity within celiac disease by comparing diagnosed and undiagnosed cases, utilizing LDSC to assess genetic heterogeneity between groups.
Developed and validated predictive machine learning models for undiagnosed celiac disease in HUNT4, comparing elastic net logistic regression, random forest, SVM, neural networks, and Super Learner ensembles (elastic net selected).
Integrated and harmonised real-world data across unique IDs from HUNT surveys, HUNT Biobank, the Norwegian Patient Registry, and clinical journal records to derive ICD-based celiac phenotypes, clinical histories, and causal estimates.
Automated end-to-end GWAS workflows with Snakemake on HUNT Cloud for reproducible analysis, and built an open-source R package migrating legacy health-analytics models into version-controlled, Dockerised pipelines.
Piloted HLA-region imputation with CookHLA and a containerised Michigan Imputation Server to extend HLA coverage in the cohort.
Prototyped a modular R/Shiny tool for Nordic HTA QALY-shortfall analysis across five Nordic countries, reducing ad-hoc requests from external partners.
Mentored two master’s students informally, collaborated with molecular biologists and clinical researchers, and secured competitive funding.

title: Indirect treatment comparisons : Part 2
text:
You have two trials, each comparing Drug C and Drug B against common comparator Drug A
Such a situation where a common comparator is present helps in anchoring the comparison and hence called Anchored Treatment Comparison.
However, Drug C is your own drug and you yourself have conducted the clinical trial for it and have individual level data for each patient randomized into the two treatment arms. Unfortunately, or ever so often you only find aggregate level data about demographics and treatment effect for the competitor’s trial. The competitor never provides detailed info of their trial.
To tackle this issue, we resort to mathematical assumptions.
Word of caution, wrong assumption might lead to a completely opposite conclusion making the worse drug look good, which would have massive consequence to the society in terms of population health and economics.
Lets us dive into the assumptions and methods

title: Indirect treatment comparisons : Part 2
text:
You have two trials, each comparing Drug C and Drug B against common comparator Drug A
Such a situation where a common comparator is present helps in anchoring the comparison and hence called Anchored Treatment Comparison.
However, Drug C is your own drug and you yourself have conducted the clinical trial for it and have individual level data for each patient randomized into the two treatment arms. Unfortunately, or ever so often you only find aggregate level data about demographics and treatment effect for the competitor’s trial. The competitor never provides detailed info of their trial.
To tackle this issue, we resort to mathematical assumptions.
Word of caution, wrong assumption might lead to a completely opposite conclusion making the worse drug look good, which would have massive consequence to the society in terms of population health and economics.
Lets us dive into the assumptions and methods

title: Indirect treatment comparisons : Part 2
text:
Standard Indirect Comparison
aka Bucher method developed by H.C. Bucher in 1997.
We would cycle back to the same example in this article.
Trial AB : Drug B - Drug A (which is treatment effect) = 20 (let us consider for now)
Trial AC : Drug C - Drug A = 15

On subtracting the two, should give us a very straight forward treatment effect difference between Drug C and Drug B which comes out to be 5 units.
However such math only hold under a massive assumption that there is absolutely no different in the effect modifying variables in the two populations.
This brings us to various important terms we would be using:







Effect modifiers
Prognostic variables




We observe from the previous example that drug B works better among 40 years old, but as one grows older their metabolism might not function the same extent as it did in their youth and hence the 70 year old patient might observe the same effect as the former patient.
A prognostic variable on the other hand are the characteristics of the patient irrespective of what treatment they receive. For eg new heart disease medication, overall baseline health/severity of atrial blockage is a prognostic variable. Since they are sicker at baseline they will have worse outcome irrespective of which drug they get. Hence these variables predict their overall prognosis.



Bucher method falls apart when effect modifiers have different distribution inches two population.
For example: Trial AB tested the effect among 40 year olds whereas Trial AC tested among predominantly 70 year olds.
In such cases you simply cannot subtract the effects, and claim one is better than other.
Even RCT does not balance out the intra-trial effect modifiers and prognostic variables. Within the respective trials we can expect the effect to average out between the intervention and the comparator arms.
Trail AB would balance everything between arm B and arm A and similar would be seen between arm C and arm A in trail AC, but to assume that effects would be balance between the trails would be a mistake.

title: Indirect treatment comparisons : Part 2
text:
Sparse networks
We rarely have dense network of RCT providing the necessary evidence. If we did then perhaps the effect would average out between these trails. However, in reality such occurrences are very rare. In HTA, we have one or two pivotal trials and standard indirect comparison (i.e. Bucher method) introduces serious systematic bias.
Let us take another example: Purely by chance you end up with more men than women compared to the general population. Then we can still assess the effects at population level by crude direct standardisation.
CDS means to get the estimates for men and women separately and then reweight the averages to match the true natural split.
Unfortunately this method does not hold in modern medical trial because human biology is multi-dimensional. So you probably need to end with adjusting for many more variables, which leads to too many buckets of very specific subgroup with very few to no patients in that stratification which then might lead to that subgroup have no patients essentially making their weight x n (=0) = 0. For example a female smoker at the age 70 might not be observered in the population and hence the crude direct standard
Paul Rosenbaum introduced propensity score matching in 1983, and the next leap of indirect treatment comparison occurred when the same principle was applied to indirect treatment comparison.
• It was fundamentally a conditional probability
• Mathematical likehood that an individual from a broader target population would be assigned to your specific trail sample given his unique characteristics.
How to achieve this? • Feed the individual level patient data into a logistic model. • Use the fitted model to predict which individuals from the external cohort are more likely to represent the previous cohort. • The \(y_{i}\) - probability for each individual in the external cohort acts as the weights. • You weight that individual with inverse of the probability that you just received.







SATE
PATE




Sample average treatment effect
Population average treatment effect


Raw unadjusted result of RCT
Ajdusteed result at population level


Effect of the drug limited to the sample of RCT
Effect of the drug as if administered to the entire population



PSM acts a bridge from SATE to PATE.
4 non-negotiable assumptions for this to hold
1) Homogeneity of the outcome irrespective of the administration in RCT/real world i.e. from contraolled environment as observed in RCT to uncontrolled environment such as the real world.
2) Outcome of one individual is indidependent or other individual. This automatically apploes to most pf the chronic disease for eg BP med given to one individual does not effect your BP meds. But it falls apart in case of infecticious disease where where if one person is vaccinated another person risk to the disease changes due to change in the herd immunity.
3) Strongly ignorable treatment assignment  - Assignment of the drug is 100% independent of any other factor. Acheiveable by double blinding.
4) Strongly ignoreable sample assignment - there are no unmeasured variable related to both how you selected your sample and the outcome of the disease.
Conditional consistency of relative effects which is when placebo is unethical because of the life threatening condition treatment off drug B must be tested against drug a however drug a was tested long back against placebo so if you study the effect modifier of something very specific such as a 50 year old female who was a smoker it should be the same irrespective of whether the effect was studied in 2015 or 2025.

title: Indirect treatment comparisons : Part 2
text:
MAIC matching adjusted indirect comparison
Trial AB: 500 individuals aged 47 to 75 years with 64% of the sample being female
Trial AC: 300 patients aged between 45 to 55 years with 80% of the sample being female
Age here is the effect modifier and sex is considered as the prognostic factor
We want to weigh 500 patients from trial AB to look like the 300 patients from trial AC MAIC bypasses the logistic regression based PSM
MAIC uses method of moments to estimate the patient weights
Where moments refer to the quantitative measure of the shape of the distribution it is a point estimate where
M1 = mean and M2 = variance
Computer algorithm searches for the unique set of weights to multiply each of the 500 individuals such that the weighted average becomes equal to the AC trial with 300 patients and the weighted standard deviation matches the published standard deviation.
The R package uses BFGH algorithm.
However age range seems to not overlap in trial AB the age ranged between 45 to 75 and in trial AC it ranged between 45 to 55
The algorithm would assign 0 weight to people who are aged 56 to 75 years old
The range of the weights seem to be from zero to 3.44 as assigned by the algorithm
However the median of the weights is 0.07 meaning half of the patients are given a weight close to 0 which implies that they are erased from the final trial but this drastically decreases the sample size and hence the power and increases the confidence interval
Another important terminology hence arises called the effective sample size the effective sample size in the above example drops from 500 to 185.6 which implies that around 60% of the samples have been dropped and hence the margin of error widens

The sandwich package
Standard variation calculation measures the spread of our raw data but here the weight is applied also carries some uncertainty. Because the algorithm had to estimate them standard error cannot be calculated the normal way because these estimates are not fixed absolute truth. Sandwich estimator accounts for error from both sources a central matrix containing the variance of the data is sandwiched between the variance of the algorithms estimate on both sides. (why both sides?)

title: Indirect treatment comparisons : Part 2
text:
Simulated treatment comparison
Take all 500 individuals put them into a regression the beta coefficient of variables states the relationship of that variable with the outcome
Now you plug the AC aggregate parameters into the regression model built on trial AB
The underlying assumption is that the shape of your statistical model is correct
For example your regression model assumes that the relation between age and outcome is a straight line but the biology says otherwise then the entire model fails and the model is called to be misspecified
$outcome is equal to treatment arm plus age plus sex
Checked residual deviance measures the variance of the data that the model equation fails to explain
When gender was added to the equation the residual deviance did not sink so adding gender did not make the model significantly better. So it is better to drop the gender from the equation.
True log odds ratio of drug C versus drug B is equal to-0.400. Which means that C is more effective than B.
If a farmer naively conducts a busher method ignoring age as a effect modifier then the treatment effect of drug C versus B is equal to 0.35 which implies that drug B is much more effective than drug C however this is contrary to what the reality is which is why nice asks for maic and STC while the MAIC of drug C versus B equals -0.032
STC of drugs C versus B equals -0.247.
Since the assumed example is framed in such a way that the distribution of the variables are known and similar in both trials hence the value of STC is closer to the real indirect treatment comparison. However this might not be the case always and it doesn’t mean that STC is universally superior especially when the relationships of the variables and the outcomes are nonlinear.
All of this happens when we have a common comparator a till now everything was called an anchored treatment effectiveness a being present allows for the randomization in both trials even if there are prognostic variables unmeasured the randomization of trial AC and trial AB ensures that they are equally balanced between treatment and control arms.
What if we have a trial comparing drug C to drug A and another trial comparing drug B to standard of care and we want to know the treatment effect difference between drug C versus drug B.
Then we have to resort to

title: Indirect treatment comparisons : Part 2
text:
Unanchored treatment comparison
MAIC or STC instead of merely adjusting treatment effects across a bridge now you are assuming you can absolutely predict biological outcomes from the mathematical covariance alone.
In anchor trials, randomization handles the prognostic variables and you only need to account for the effect modifiers.
In unanchored trials you need to adjust for both but account for all prognostic variables is very difficult example genetic predisposition gut microbiome etc. The harsh reality is that you cannot. Unanchored estimates suffers inherently from an unknown amount of bias that is where the next method comes in.

title: Indirect treatment comparisons : Part 2
text:
Doubly robust estimator
This combines both MAIC and STC.
PSM for weights of patients simultaneously build an outcome regression model to predict the results based on covariance. As long as anyone is consistent the final estimate would be reliable if PSM fails to assign accurate weights but the outcome regression model captures the biological relation correctly or vice versa then you are protected.
Regression model should reflect the biological distribution and hence the treatment effect and not the additive on natural scale but rather on a transformed scale either log or biologically plausible transformative scale.
This still leaves us with target population paradox.
Which states that Drug A is trying to prove that it is better than Drug B. However, it should prove that it is better for the entire UK population.

title: Understanding the spatial predictors of malnutrition among 0–2 years children in India using path analysis
text:
Abstract
Despite several programs and policies to turn down the burden of malnutrition in the country, the rank of India in the Global Hunger Index (GHI) is 102 among 117 countries, which indicates a serious hunger situation. It is essential to design more specific interventions by focusing on the key determinants that may directly or indirectly influence malnutrition in India.
Utilizing data from the National Family and Health Survey-4 (NFHS) (2015-16), we developed a structural equation model to find the direct, indirect, and total effect of various determinants on stunting, wasting, and underweight. We used spatial analysis to identify local occurrences of factors that are critical in controlling malnutrition. A p-value of 0.05 was considered to be significant throughout the study. Analysis was performed using STATA (version 15.1MP) and GeoDa software (version 1.14).
A final sample of 90, 842 children of 0-24 months of age was selected for the analysis. The CFI and TLI values of 0.98 and 0.93, respectively, are indicative of a good fit model. Moran’s I value of global spatial autocorrelation for the widespread presence of diarrhea, poor drinking water source, exclusive breastfeeding, low birth weight, no prenatal visits, poor toilet facility was observed to be 0.446, 0.638, 0.345, 0.439, 0.620, and 0.727, respectively.
A robust direct relation was observed for diarrhea, exclusive breastfeeding, and children born with stunting, underweight, and wasting. The variables associated indirectly with the outcome variables were the education of the mother, residence, and desired pregnancy. The identification of hotspots through spatial analysis would help revive control strategies in the affected area according to geographical needs. It is extensively addressed that interventions related to health and nutrition during the first 1, 000 days of life is crucial to seize the upshoot of growth floundering among children.

title: Genetic differences between diagnosed and undiagnosed Celiac disease: a population-based study
text:
Abstract
A large proportion of individuals with celiac disease (CeD) remain undiagnosed, often presenting at an older age of onset or with non-classical symptoms compared to diagnosed cases. Such heterogeneity might be related to genetic factors. The aim was to utilize a CeD-screened adult population to compare the genetic variants in known and newly diagnosed cases. In the fourth wave of the population-based Trøndelag Health Study (HUNT4) 826 CeD and 51,516 non-CeD individuals were included. Medical registries identified 361 previously diagnosed cases, while screening identified 465 new cases. A validated polygenic risk score (PRS) was used to assess the genetic risk of CeD among the two case groups versus non-CeD individuals. Additional genetic variants not included in the PRS were also analyzed. The PRS distinguished cases from non-cases with high accuracy (AUROC: 85% for known cases, 83% for new cases). The genetic variation explained by the PRS was similar for known and new cases (17.1% versus 14.5%). The odds ratio for being in the highest genetic risk group (top 10%) was 22.7 (95% CI 14.1–36.4) for known cases and 18.6 (95% CI 12.4–27.9) for new cases versus the median group (40%-60%). Differences in effect size among specific genome-wide variants were observed but were not significantly associated with CeD. A validated PRS showed significant genetic difference between CeD cases and the general population, with similar association in both known and newly diagnosed cases. This suggests that genetic architectures of the two groups are comparable, implying that other non-genetic factors may drive CeD in adults.

title: The IRX1 locus is associated with celiac disease: results from a screened population-based cohort, the HUNT study.
text:
Abstract
Previous studies have uncovered genetic loci associated with celiac disease (CeD) within both the human leukocyte antigen (HLA) and non-HLA regions. However, half of the heritability remains unexplained. This study aimed to identify novel loci associated with CeD in a general adult population screened for the disease, mitigating the likely selection bias observed in previous case-control studies. The study utilized data from the fourth Trøndelag Health Study (HUNT4) in Norway, where 52,358 adults were screened for CeD using serology, identifying 465 previously undiagnosed biopsy- confirmed cases. Additionally, 377 previously diagnosed cases were identified through hospital journal searches and registry data. Genotyping of 373,185 single nucleotide polymorphisms was performed on all participant using four Illumina HumanCoreExome arrays. Imputation, using the Haplotype Reference Consortium panel, resulted in approximately 24.9 million variants, post quality control. A genome-wide association study was performed using SAIGE, and functional mapping and pathway enrichment analysis was conducted using FUMA. All except one of the 42 known autosomal loci were present in the data, of which seven reached the suggestive significance threshold (P≤ 5 x 10-6). Thirteen independent novel associations were observed (P ≤ 5x 10-8), with the 5p15.33 locus showing the highest potential for a true association with CeD, warranting further studies to validate the findings. Notably, the IRX1 gene, located close to the 5p15.33 locus has also been associated with rheumatoid arthritis, suggesting a new shared autoimmune locus.

title: Thyroid function test in COVID-19 patients: a cross-sectional study in a tertiary care hospital
text:
Abstract
Context: There is scarcity of data on thyroid function abnormality in COVID-19 patients in world literature.
Aims: The objective of this study was to assess thyroid function tests in hospitalized patients of COVID-19.
Settings and Design: Sixty (60) patients with COVID-19 detected by RT-PCR admitted in General Medicine isolation ward and COVID block of a tertiary care teaching hospital were selected by semi-purposive sampling.
Materials and Methods: These patients were assessed for thyroid function tests, including total T3, free T3, total T4, free T4, TSH and anti-TPO antibody along with other baseline investigations. Patients with pre-existing thyroid–related ailments, those on levothyroxine or anti-thyroid drugs or other drugs known to interfere with the results were excluded.
Results: There were 43.3% patients in mild, 26.7% in moderate, and 30% in severe category, according to local COVID-19 severity classification protocol. 35% patients had one or more abnormality in the thyroid function, low TSH being the most common (18.33%). 9.1% patients had characteristic pattern of thyroiditis. In most of the others thyroid function did not match any typical pattern. There was no significant difference in any of the parameters of the thyroid function test between mild, moderate, and severe groups.
Conclusion: Thyroid function may be abnormal in all categories of patients during COVID-19 infection, even in absence of pre-existing thyroid ailments. Although low TSH is the commonest abnormality and typical pattern of thyroiditis can be seen in a subsection of patients, in majority of the patients, thyroid function abnormality does not follow any characteristic pattern and likely represents a combination of thyroiditis and sick euthyroid syndrome in different points of its spectrum.

title: A model for predicting celiac disease among undiagnosed subjects established with data from the HUNT4 study
text:
Abstract
Celiac disease (CeD) is an immune mediated disorder with substantial underdiagnosis, particularly in adults with non-specific symptoms. Universal population screening remains under debate due to cost-effectiveness and potential quality-of-life implications. Clinical prediction tools aid clinicians in identifying individuals who might benefit from targeted screening.
Using data from 52,000 adults in the fourth population-based Trøndelag Health Study (HUNT4) in Norway, we developed and internally validated a non-diagnostic prediction model for previously undiagnosed CeD. The model incorporated predictors spanning genetics, lifestyle, symptoms, comorbidity, and biomarkers. Elastic-net logistic regression with nested cross-validation was chosen due to the low disease prevalence and imbalanced case-control distribution. Model performance was assessed by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, area under precision-recall curve, and calibration plots. Clinical utility was evaluated at different risk thresholds.
Among 465 newly diagnosed cases and 51,515 controls, polygenic risk score emerged as the strongest predictor for CeD, alongside diabetic history, kidney function, chronic discomfort, and perceived health status. The model achieved high discrimination (84%) and good calibration (0.009). The model outperformed universal population screening by detecting more cases, especially when the predicted risk was less than 2%. Increasing sample prevalence for sensitivity analysis, revealed that the model was better in population scenarios compared to high-risk/high-prevalence scenarios.
The multifactorial model demonstrated strong potential for guiding targeted screening for CeD, especially in low-prevalence, true population-based settings. While not a diagnostic tool, it may support clinical decision-making by identifying individuals at elevated risk. External validation and cost-effectiveness studies are needed before it can be implemented in primary care.

title: Population screening of adults identifies novel genetic variants associated with celiac disease
text:
Abstract
Celiac disease (CeD) is an autoimmune disease driven by a complex genetic interplay within and beyond the human leukocyte antigen (HLA) region. Despite this, half of its heritability remains unexplained, with most of the unidentified variants located in non-protein coding regions. Here we performed a genome-wide association study among 52,342 adults screened for CeD, including 465 previously undiagnosed and 361 already diagnosed cases, which mitigated the likely disease misclassification present in previous studies. Genotyping and imputation yielded approximately 24.9 million variants for analysis. The study identified 15 novel associations (P < 5E-08) in 12 loci in addition to all the previously associated loci at lower significance thresholds (P < 5E-03). The 5p15.33 locus in the long non-coding RNA gene (LINC01019) showed the highest potential for a true association with CeD. Notably, variants in 5p15.33 has also been associated with rheumatoid arthritis, suggesting a new shared autoimmune locus.

title: Impact of transitioning to newer utility on sex-specific quality-adjusted life expectancy in Norway
text:
Abstract
Norway has mandated the adoption of the new Norwegian EQ-5D-5L value set from September 1, 2025. This transition change was long overdue, as the former value set was based on decades old assessment of health-related quality of life.
Current study disseminates the updated quality-adjusted life expectancies (QALE) for the Norwegian population based on age and sex, and quantify how the new norm alters the absolute and proportional shortfall in QALY.
The population norm derived from the general population survey by Garratt et al., 2021 has been linked to the most recent Norwegian Lifetable (2023-2024) to estimate the QALE using the Sullivan method. It is compared to the van Hout et al.’s crosswalk QALE norms on the same lifetable. Variable discount rates were applied at 4%, 3% and 2% as per guidelines.
Based on the newer population norms the QALE of average population has decreased by 4%. The QALE at birth was previous 69.62 years for men and 69.67 years for women which came down to 64.93 years and 68.77 years respectively.
The current study quantifies the diminishing QALEs based on the updated QALE estimates at the same time allowing the estimation of absolute and proportional shortfall.

title: Hi there!
text:
I currently work as an health economist at PenTAG, University of Exeter, UK.
I appraise health economic evidence and models submitted as part of single technology assessment (STA) to the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) in the UK. Alongside appraisals, I also build de novo / adapt guidance health economic models as part of multiple techonology assessment or consultancy projects.



Picture taken on way to Norwegian course to Dragvoll campus.


Prior to joining PenTAG, I completed my PhD in Genetic Epidemiology from Norwegian University of Science and Technology(NTNU), at the beautiful city of Trondheim 🏔🫎🫐 in Norway 🇳🇴 🥹.
My PhD research focused on developing and applying statistical methods for genetic association studies, poslygenic risk scores with a particular emphasis on autoimmune disease. And prior to my PhD, I worked as an Associate in the Advanced Analytics team at Parexel, providing consulting services to pharmaceutical companies 💊. I worked on various health economic and outcomes research (HEOR) projects, including cost-effectiveness analysis, indirect treatment comparisons, and regressional and survival analysis.
